lessons.title: Course Introduction: Becoming an Azure Database Administrator
SQL Server On-Prem vs. Azure SQL — Understanding the Ecosystem

slots.practicalActivity: Sign in to the Azure Portal with a free or existing subscription and browse to the SQL databases and Azure SQL Managed Instance service blades without creating anything yet. For each on-prem concept you already administered in the SQL Server DBA courses (instance, database, login, Agent job), write down what the Azure equivalent is called and where you'd find it in the Portal.
slots.deliverable: A one-page on-prem-to-Azure terminology map (instance to logical server, Agent job to Elastic Job/Azure Automation, etc.) saved as azure-vs-onprem-map.md.

lessons.title: Azure SQL Database vs. Managed Instance vs. SQL Server on Azure VM
IaaS vs. PaaS for SQL Server

slots.practicalActivity: In the Azure Portal's Create a resource search, open the create blades for Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, and SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines side by side (without finishing creation) and note the different required fields each one asks for. Then decide, for three realistic scenarios — a small departmental web app, a lift-and-shift of an on-prem instance with linked servers and Agent jobs, and a dev/test box — which of the three options fits and whether it's IaaS or PaaS.
slots.deliverable: A short decision table with one row per scenario naming the chosen deployment option and a one-sentence IaaS/PaaS justification for each.

lessons.title: Azure Portal, SSMS & Azure Data Studio for DBAs
Lab: Build Your First Azure SQL Environment

slots.practicalActivity: Open SSMS and Azure Data Studio side by side, then follow the lab exactly: in the Azure Portal, create resource group rg-azure-dba-lab, deploy a single Azure SQL Database (smallest DTU tier) with a new logical server, add a firewall rule for your own client IP under the server's Networking blade, connect to it from SSMS, and run SELECT DB_NAME(), @@SERVERNAME, SERVERPROPERTY('Edition') to prove the Portal deployment, firewall rule, and SSMS connection all actually work together.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of the successful query result showing the 'SQL Azure' edition string, plus a lab-notes.md listing the exact resource group, server, and database names used.

lessons.title: Azure SQL Purchasing Models, Service Tiers & Compute Options

slots.practicalActivity: Using the Azure CLI (az sql server create and az sql db create), recreate the same logical-server-then-database hierarchy from the previous lab, but name the resource group rg-azure-dba-ch2 and give the server a globally-unique name following a real naming convention (e.g. sql-azuredba-<yourinitials>-ch2). Then open the database's pricing tier blade and compare the DTU-based Basic/Standard/Premium tiers against the vCore General Purpose/Business Critical tiers shown for the same database.
slots.deliverable: The two CLI commands run (saved as deploy-ch2.sh or .ps1) plus a short note on which purchasing model and tier you'd recommend for a production OLTP app and why.

lessons.title: DTU vs. vCore & Choosing the Right Database Configuration

slots.practicalActivity: On the database created in the previous slot, open the Compute + storage configuration blade and toggle between the DTU model and the vCore model, recording what changes (compute size options, max storage, cost estimate shown). Then switch the database to Serverless compute, set an auto-pause delay, and sketch how you'd group 4 departmental databases with unpredictable, non-overlapping usage into a single elastic pool instead of giving each one fixed DTUs.
slots.deliverable: A short comparison note (DTU vs. vCore, provisioned vs. serverless) plus a one-paragraph elastic-pool sizing recommendation for the 4-database scenario.

lessons.title: Azure SQL Managed Instance Deployment & Configuration
SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines & Hybrid SQL

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab database, open the Compute + storage blade and perform a live scale-up (increase vCores or DTUs), noting the brief impact Azure warns about before confirming. Then start (without necessarily finishing, given cost) the Create Azure SQL Managed Instance wizard to see its required subnet/VNet fields, and read through the SQL Server on Azure VM marketplace image's size/storage options to compare what 'you manage everything' really means versus Managed Instance.
slots.deliverable: A one-page note comparing what you'd personally have to manage in each of the three deployment options (storage scaling, OS patching, backups), based on what the wizards actually asked you to configure.

lessons.title: Choosing the Correct Azure SQL Solution for Business Requirements

slots.practicalActivity: Given a hypothetical 2TB sales-history database that's slow to query and growing fast, decide and justify which Azure SQL option fits, then design a partitioning scheme for its largest fact-style table (e.g. partition by order date, one partition per quarter) and write the CREATE PARTITION FUNCTION / CREATE PARTITION SCHEME T-SQL you would run against it.
slots.deliverable: A .sql script with a working partition function and partition scheme definition for a date-based partitioning strategy, plus a one-paragraph justification for the Azure SQL option chosen.

slots.practicalActivity: On a lab database, run sp_estimate_data_compression_savings against one of your larger tables, then apply PAGE compression with ALTER TABLE ... REBUILD WITH (DATA_COMPRESSION = PAGE) and compare before/after size using sp_spaceused. Separately, sketch a sharding design for a multi-tenant table (e.g. shard by CustomerID range or hash) and note which query pattern would become harder once rows are split across shards.
slots.deliverable: A before/after sp_spaceused comparison showing the compression savings, plus a one-paragraph sharding design note identifying at least one query pattern that gets harder under that shard key.

lessons.title: Azure Arc, Hybrid SQL & Azure SQL Database in Microsoft Fabric

slots.practicalActivity: In the Azure Portal, browse the options for enabling Azure Arc on a hypothetical on-prem SQL Server instance and for connecting an Azure SQL Database to Microsoft Fabric as a mirrored source, without necessarily completing either. Write down, in your own words, what problem each one solves that plain Azure SQL doesn't.
slots.deliverable: A short note explaining, in plain language, why a company with on-prem SQL Server would adopt Azure Arc, and why a company already on Azure SQL Database would mirror it into Fabric.

lessons.title: SQL Authentication vs. Microsoft Entra Authentication
Configuring Microsoft Entra ID for Azure SQL

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab Azure SQL Database, enable Microsoft Entra authentication by setting an Entra admin in the Portal's Microsoft Entra ID blade, then connect to the database from SSMS twice — once with the original SQL authentication login, once using Entra authentication with your Entra account — and compare the two sign-in experiences.
slots.deliverable: Screenshots of both successful connections (SQL auth and Entra auth) plus a one-paragraph note on why Entra authentication removes the need to manage a separate SQL password for that login.

lessons.title: Server Roles, Database Roles & Object Permissions

slots.practicalActivity: Using T-SQL, create a new SQL login and database user, add that user to the built-in db_datareader role, then create a custom database role, grant it SELECT and EXECUTE at the schema level, and add the same user to it. Confirm the effective permissions difference between the two role memberships by querying sys.database_permissions.
slots.deliverable: A .sql script creating the login, user, custom role, and role memberships, plus a short comment block explaining what each grant actually allows.

slots.practicalActivity: Write explicit GRANT, DENY, and REVOKE statements against a lab table or stored procedure for a test user, then query sys.database_permissions to confirm DENY overrides a GRANT from role membership. Apply the principle of least privilege by auditing one existing lab login's permissions and removing any grant wider than that login actually needs (e.g. db_owner on a login that only runs reports).
slots.deliverable: A .sql script showing the GRANT/DENY/REVOKE statements and the sys.database_permissions query confirming DENY wins, plus a short before/after note on the least-privilege cleanup made.

slots.practicalActivity: Deliberately break a connection by creating a SQL login with no corresponding database user, attempting to connect, and reading the exact error number/message SSMS returns; then fix it by mapping the login to a user with CREATE USER ... FOR LOGIN. Repeat with a permissions error (connect as a user with no SELECT rights on a table) and resolve it.
slots.deliverable: A troubleshooting log noting the two error messages reproduced, their error numbers, and the exact T-SQL fix for each.

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab Azure SQL Server, open the Networking blade, review the current firewall rules, add a second rule for another IP, then uncheck 'Allow Azure services and resources to access this server' and observe the effect on your own SSMS connection. Separately, review the VNet + service endpoint configuration screen and note which subnet-level setting would let a VM in a specific VNet reach the database without a public IP.
slots.deliverable: A short note recording what happened to the SSMS connection when 'Allow Azure services' was unchecked, plus the exact subnet setting name required for a VNet service endpoint.

slots.practicalActivity: In the Portal, open the Private endpoint connections blade for your lab server and walk through the private endpoint creation wizard far enough to see which VNet/subnet/private DNS zone fields it requires, then compare that to the public-endpoint-plus-firewall-rule setup you already have. Write a short decision note on which connectivity model you'd use for a database holding customer PII.
slots.deliverable: A one-paragraph decision note recommending public vs. private connectivity for a PII-holding database, naming the specific private endpoint fields seen in the wizard.

slots.practicalActivity: Deliberately misconfigure your own connectivity (remove your IP from the firewall rules, or use the wrong server FQDN) and capture the exact SSMS error message and error number for each failure, then fix each one and reconnect successfully.
slots.deliverable: A troubleshooting log pairing each deliberate misconfiguration with its exact error message/number and the fix that resolved it.

lessons.title: Always Encrypted & Always Encrypted with Secure Enclaves

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab database, confirm Transparent Data Encryption is enabled via the Transparent data encryption blade, then run sys.dm_database_encryption_keys to see the encryption state in T-SQL. Separately, read through the Always Encrypted wizard in SSMS far enough to see which two key types (column master key, column encryption key) it asks you to generate for a sensitive column like SSN or CreditCardNumber.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot or query result confirming TDE is enabled on the database, plus a short note naming the two key types Always Encrypted requires and which one never leaves the client.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a dynamic data mask on a sensitive column (e.g. a partial mask on an email or phone column) with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... ADD MASKED WITH (FUNCTION = ...), then query the table as a low-privilege user to confirm the mask applies, and as a user with UNMASK permission to confirm it doesn't. Then enable Row-Level Security on a table with a security predicate function that restricts rows to a specific RegionID, and test it under two different session contexts.
slots.deliverable: A .sql script with the masked column definition, the RLS security policy and predicate function, and two query results (masked/unmasked, filtered/unfiltered) proving each control works.

slots.practicalActivity: Run the Data Discovery & Classification scan in the Portal on your lab database and review which columns it automatically flags as sensitive. Separately, enable SQL Auditing to a storage account or Log Analytics workspace, generate some sample activity (a few SELECTs and an UPDATE), and confirm the events show up in the audit log.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of the Data Discovery scan results plus a screenshot of at least 3 captured audit log entries confirming auditing is active.

slots.practicalActivity: Enable system-versioned temporal tables (row history tracking) on one lab table, make several UPDATEs to a row, then query the table's history using FOR SYSTEM_TIME ALL to see every prior version. Write a short note on how this differs from database ledger's tamper-evidence guarantee.
slots.deliverable: A query result showing the temporal history of an updated row, plus a one-paragraph note distinguishing temporal tables (change history) from ledger (tamper-evidence).

lessons.title: Understanding Database Monitoring & Creating a Performance Baseline

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab database, open the Metrics blade in Azure Monitor and chart DTU/vCore percentage, Data IO percentage, and successful/failed connections over the last hour while running a few test queries, then create a metric alert rule that fires when CPU percentage exceeds a threshold. Write down what you'd consider a healthy baseline for this lab database based on what the charts show at idle.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of the Azure Monitor metrics chart plus the alert rule configuration (metric, threshold, action group) created.

slots.practicalActivity: If Database Watcher is available in your subscription/region, open it against your lab database and review its built-in dashboards; otherwise compare its documented views to running sys.dm_exec_requests and sys.dm_os_wait_stats directly via T-SQL against the same database. Write 3 DMV queries that answer 'what's running right now' and 'what is the server waiting on.'
slots.deliverable: 3 working DMV queries (active requests, wait stats, and one more of your choosing) saved as a .sql file with a one-line comment above each explaining what question it answers.

lessons.title: Monitoring Sessions, Connections, CPU, Memory, I/O & Storage

slots.practicalActivity: Create an Extended Events session on your lab database that captures sql_statement_completed events with a duration filter (only statements over 100ms), start it, run a few queries against your lab tables, then watch the live data in SSMS's Extended Events viewer. Separately, query sys.dm_exec_sessions and sys.dm_exec_connections for current connections, and sys.dm_os_performance_counters for a CPU/memory counter.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of the Extended Events live data showing at least one captured statement, plus the sys.dm_exec_sessions query result listing your own active session.

lessons.title: Reading Execution Plans for Performance Problems

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one of your more complex lab queries (a join across 2-3 tables), run it with Include Actual Execution Plan turned on in SSMS, and walk the methodology: check wait stats first (sys.dm_os_wait_stats), then the plan itself, identifying the most expensive operator by percentage cost.
slots.deliverable: A saved .sqlplan file (or screenshot) of the execution plan with the most expensive operator noted, plus a one-paragraph write-up of what was checked and in what order.

lessons.title: Index Seeks, Scans, Lookups & Common Plan Operators

slots.practicalActivity: In that same execution plan, identify every Index Seek, Scan, and Key Lookup operator and note which one costs the most. Then run sys.dm_db_missing_index_details against your lab database, create the single highest-impact suggested index, and re-run the query to confirm the plan now shows a Seek instead of a Scan.
slots.deliverable: A before/after execution plan comparison (Scan to Seek) plus the CREATE INDEX statement that made the difference.

lessons.title: Using Query Store to Find Regressed Queries

slots.practicalActivity: Confirm Query Store is enabled on your lab database and review its retention/capture settings, run a query a few times, then open the Top Resource Consuming Queries report in SSMS. Deliberately make the query slower (e.g. wrap an indexed column in a function to break SARGability), run it again, and use the Regressed Queries report to spot the regression and force the prior good plan.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of the Regressed Queries report showing the before/after plan, plus a note on whether the old plan was forced or the query was fixed instead.

slots.practicalActivity: In two SSMS query windows against the same lab table, start a transaction in window 1 that updates a row without committing, then run a conflicting UPDATE in window 2 and observe the block using sys.dm_exec_requests and sys.dm_tran_locks. Commit window 1, confirm window 2 completes, then deliberately reproduce a deadlock between two transactions updating rows in opposite order and capture the deadlock graph.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of the blocking session pair (blocking_session_id) from sys.dm_exec_requests, plus a captured deadlock graph from the reproduced deadlock.

slots.practicalActivity: Check whether Intelligent Query Processing features are active on your lab database via compatibility level, then review the Automatic Tuning blade in the Portal and enable Force Last Good Plan if it isn't already, explaining in your own words how it would behave the next time a plan regresses like the one forced manually in the previous slot.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of the Automatic Tuning settings with Force Last Good Plan enabled, plus a short note on how it differs from manually forcing a plan via Query Store.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Query Performance Tuning: pick one of the slowest lab queries from earlier in this chapter and run the full troubleshooting methodology against it start to finish — wait stats, execution plan, missing/unused index check, Query Store regression check — documenting what was found and fixed at each step, even where the answer was 'nothing wrong here.'
slots.deliverable: A tuning report walking through all four methodology steps against one real query, with before/after evidence (plan, index, or Query Store screenshot) for whichever step actually fixed something.

slots.practicalActivity: Query sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats against your lab database to find the fragmentation percentage of your indexes, then rebuild or reorganize the most fragmented one based on the standard >30%/5-30% thresholds. Separately, check sys.dm_db_stats_properties for a table's statistics and manually run UPDATE STATISTICS on it, comparing the last-updated timestamp before and after.
slots.deliverable: A before/after fragmentation query result showing the rebuilt/reorganized index, plus the UPDATE STATISTICS confirmation.

slots.practicalActivity: Run DBCC CHECKDB against your lab database and review the output for any integrity errors (there shouldn't be any, which is itself worth confirming). Then open the database-scoped configuration options with ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION and change one setting such as MAXDOP, explaining what server-level vs. database-scoped actually means for that setting on Azure SQL.
slots.deliverable: The DBCC CHECKDB output confirming 0 allocation/consistency errors, plus the ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION statement run and a one-line explanation of what it changed.

slots.practicalActivity: Sketch a workload-isolation scenario on paper using Azure SQL's per-database resource caps/elastic pool limits to simulate capping one noisy workload (the Resource Governor equivalent for PaaS). Then scale your lab database up and back down via the Portal or CLI, timing how long each scaling operation takes and noting any brief connection drop.
slots.deliverable: A short note describing the workload-isolation approach for Azure SQL (per-database resource caps/elastic pool) plus timing notes from the actual scale-up/scale-down test.

slots.practicalActivity: On an on-prem or VM-hosted SQL Server instance (or an Agent-capable Managed Instance), create a new SQL Server Agent job with two steps — a T-SQL step running a simple maintenance query and a second step that only runs on success — and attach a daily schedule to it. Run the job manually and review the job history.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of the job's step configuration and schedule, plus the job history output showing a successful run.

slots.practicalActivity: Configure a SQL Server Agent operator with your own email (or a test address) and attach it to an alert that fires on a specific error severity (severity 16+), then deliberately fail one of the job's steps (point it at a nonexistent table) and review the resulting job history failure message and whether the alert/notification fired.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of the failed job step's error message plus the operator/alert configuration set up to be notified of it.

lessons.title: Building a DBA Maintenance & Monitoring Strategy

slots.practicalActivity: Build a single Agent job that chains together an index maintenance step, a statistics update step, and a DBCC CHECKDB step in sequence, with each step configured to go to the next step on success and quit the job reporting failure on error. Document this as the first entry in a written DBA maintenance and monitoring strategy covering backup cadence, index/stats maintenance cadence, and integrity check cadence.
slots.deliverable: The multi-step Agent job definition (or its generated T-SQL script) plus a one-page written maintenance strategy document covering at least backups, index/stats, and integrity checks.

lessons.title: Azure CLI & PowerShell for Database Administrators

slots.practicalActivity: Using the Azure CLI, write a short script that creates a firewall rule, scales a database's service objective, and lists all databases on a logical server (az sql db list) — the same three Portal actions done manually in earlier chapters, now scripted. Then perform the same three actions with the Az PowerShell module (New-AzSqlServerFirewallRule, Set-AzSqlDatabase, Get-AzSqlDatabase) to compare the two tools' syntax for identical operations.
slots.deliverable: Two scripts (one Azure CLI, one Az PowerShell) that each perform the same three administrative actions against your lab server/database.

lessons.title: ARM Templates & Bicep for Azure SQL

slots.practicalActivity: Write a minimal Bicep file that declares an Azure SQL logical server and a database resource (mirroring the az sql server/db create commands from Chapter 2), then run az deployment group what-if against it to preview the change before actually deploying. Separately, read through the Elastic Jobs creation flow and sketch a job that would run the same index-maintenance script across every database in an elastic pool.
slots.deliverable: A working .bicep file for a server+database pair, the what-if output confirming what it would create, and a short note on how an Elastic Job would target multiple databases at once.

slots.practicalActivity: Deliberately introduce an error into the Bicep file from the previous slot (e.g. an invalid SKU name) and run the deployment to capture the exact Azure error message, then fix it and redeploy successfully. Set up an Azure Monitor action group that would alert you by email if a future automated deployment failed.
slots.deliverable: The captured deployment error message and its fix, plus the action group configuration created for deployment failure alerts.

lessons.title: Planning a SQL Server Migration to Azure

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a hypothetical on-prem SQL Server instance (or one from an earlier course) and run the Data Migration Assistant, or at minimum review its assessment report categories, to identify compatibility issues and feature parity gaps before migrating it to Azure SQL. Write a one-page migration plan naming the target option and justifying it against the assessment findings.
slots.deliverable: A one-page migration plan naming the chosen target and summarizing at least 2 real compatibility findings from the assessment.

lessons.title: Migrating SQL Server to Azure SQL Database

slots.practicalActivity: Compare the online vs. offline migration options available in Azure Database Migration Service for your planned scenario, then actually migrate a small lab database to Azure SQL Database using the Export/Import (BACPAC) method via SSMS's Export Data-tier Application wizard, confirming every table and row count matches on the target.
slots.deliverable: The exported .bacpac file (or its file name/size) plus a row-count comparison table confirming source and target match for every table.

lessons.title: Migrating to Azure SQL Managed Instance

slots.practicalActivity: If you have access to an Azure SQL Managed Instance, perform a backup/restore-based migration path appropriate to MI; otherwise walk through the Managed Instance migration wizard far enough to document its required fields. Then validate the migration by re-running a few known-good queries from the T-SQL Development course against the migrated database and confirming identical results.
slots.deliverable: A post-migration validation report listing at least 3 queries re-run against the migrated database with matching results, plus a note on any migration-specific error that had to be troubleshot.

lessons.title: SQL Server Backup Fundamentals: Full, Differential & Log
Backup & Restore with SSMS and T-SQL

slots.practicalActivity: On an on-prem or VM-hosted SQL Server, run a full backup, a differential backup, and a transaction log backup of a lab database with WITH COMPRESSION, then restore all three in the correct order using WITH NORECOVERY on every step except the last, which uses WITH RECOVERY. Confirm the database comes back online and is query-able.
slots.deliverable: The full BACKUP/RESTORE .sql script run (3 backups, 3 restores) plus a query result proving the restored database is online and queryable.

slots.practicalActivity: On your Azure SQL Database (PaaS), review the Backups blade to see Azure's automatic backup schedule and current retention, then perform a point-in-time restore to a timestamp from earlier today into a new database name, and confirm the restored copy reflects the state at that point in time (e.g. a row later deleted is still present).
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of the completed point-in-time restore operation plus a query proving the restored database reflects an earlier state than the live one.

lessons.title: Backup to Azure Storage & Disaster Recovery Scenarios

slots.practicalActivity: Configure a long-term retention policy on your Azure SQL Database (e.g. keep weekly backups for 1 year) via the Portal, and separately take a full on-prem-style backup directly to an Azure Storage account using BACKUP DATABASE ... TO URL, confirming the .bak file actually lands in the storage container.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of the configured long-term retention policy plus confirmation (storage account blob listing or Portal screenshot) that the BACKUP ... TO URL file exists in the container.

lessons.title: RPO & RTO — Designing from Business Requirements

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-page comparison distinguishing HA (staying up through a failure) from DR (recovering after a disaster that takes out a whole region), then, for a hypothetical finance application, decide what RPO and RTO you'd negotiate with the business and translate those numbers into a concrete backup/replica frequency (e.g. an RPO of 5 minutes implies log backups or synchronous replicas, not nightly fulls).
slots.deliverable: A one-page HA-vs-DR note plus a worked RPO/RTO example translating stated business numbers into a specific backup or replication frequency.

slots.practicalActivity: If multiple SQL Server instances (VMs or a lab cluster) are available, configure a 2-node Always On Availability Group with one synchronous automatic-failover replica, add a database to it, and run ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP ... FAILOVER to fail over manually, confirming the former secondary now accepts writes. If an FCI can't be built, instead diagram how its shared-storage failover differs from the AG's separate-storage replica model.
slots.deliverable: Either the AG creation script plus confirmation of a successful manual failover, or a diagram/note contrasting FCI's shared-storage model against the AG configured.

slots.practicalActivity: On an Azure SQL Database, set up Active Geo-Replication to a secondary region, confirm data is replicating by writing a row on the primary and reading it on the secondary, then perform a planned failover (promote the secondary) and confirm the original primary is now the readable secondary. Separately, configure an Azure SQL Failover Group over the database and test its failover behavior.
slots.deliverable: Confirmation (query results from both regions) that geo-replication worked and failed over successfully, plus the Failover Group configuration created.

slots.practicalActivity: If on-prem/VM SQL Server is available, configure log shipping from a primary to a secondary (restore WITH STANDBY or NORECOVERY), confirming each shipped log backup actually applies on the secondary. Then build a short HA/DR monitoring checklist (AG dashboard health, geo-replication lag, failover group health) and deliberately break one component (e.g. pause log shipping) to confirm the checklist actually catches it.
slots.deliverable: Confirmation that log shipping applied at least 2 log backups to the secondary, plus an HA/DR monitoring checklist proved to catch a deliberately broken component.

slots.practicalActivity: Read the project scenario and treat your own lab environment as the client environment: using everything from Chapters 1-6, migrate a sample on-prem-style database into Azure SQL Database, configure Entra authentication and least-privilege roles for at least two different user types, and enable TDE and auditing on it as the 'secure the environment' phase of the project.
slots.deliverable: A migrated, secured lab database with Entra auth configured, at least 2 roles with least-privilege permissions, and auditing enabled, documented in a short project log.

slots.practicalActivity: Continuing the same project database, apply the Chapter 8-9 performance methodology to find and fix at least one real tuning opportunity, automate one recurring maintenance task with an Agent job or Azure Automation script, then simulate a disaster (deliberately fail over a configured replica/failover group, or restore from a point-in-time backup as if the primary were lost) and document how long recovery actually took versus a stated RTO.
slots.deliverable: A project wrap-up report covering the performance fix made, the automation script added, and the measured recovery time from the simulated disaster, compared against a stated RTO target.

lessons.title: DP-300 Complete Exam Review & Practice Assessment

slots.practicalActivity: Take a full timed DP-300-style practice assessment covering the same domains this course mapped to (deploying/configuring, HA/DR/security, monitoring/optimizing), then for every missed question, go back to the specific lesson in this course that covers it and write one sentence on what was misunderstood.
slots.deliverable: Your practice assessment score by domain, plus a missed-question log mapping each wrong answer to the course lesson that covers it.

slots.practicalActivity: Rehearse out loud (recording yourself if possible) answers to 5 realistic Azure DBA interview questions spanning this course's range — choosing between Database/Managed Instance/VM, an AG failover scenario, a security/least-privilege scenario, troubleshooting a blocked query, and a behavioral 'tell me about a time' question — timing each answer to under 2 minutes.
slots.deliverable: Written notes (or a recording) of 5 rehearsed interview answers, each under 2 minutes.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can deploy, secure, monitor, tune, back up, and fail over Azure SQL databases end to end -- choosing the right deployment option, enforcing least-privilege access, diagnosing slow queries with execution plans and Query Store, automating routine maintenance, and designing an HA/DR strategy that meets a stated RPO/RTO -- the day-to-day, DP-300-aligned skill set of an Azure Database Administrator.
